# Psalm 88 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Translator:** SOPHIA (Council Arbiter) | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A)

---

**1** A Song. A Psalm of the Sons of Korah. To the choirmaster: according to Mahalath Leannoth. A Maskil of Heman the Ezrahite.

**2** O LORD, God of my salvation, I cry out day and night before you.

**3** Let my prayer come before you; incline your ear to my cry!

**4** For my soul is full of troubles, and my life draws near to Sheol.

**5** I am counted among those who go down to the pit; I am a man who has no strength,

**6** like one set loose among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, like those whom you remember no more, for they are cut off from your hand.

**7** You have put me in the depths of the pit, in the regions dark and deep.

**8** Your wrath lies heavy upon me, and you overwhelm me with all your waves. Selah

**9** You have caused my companions to shun me; you have made me a horror to them. I am shut in so that I cannot escape;

**10** my eye grows dim through sorrow. Every day I call upon you, O LORD; I spread out my hands to you.

**11** Do you work wonders for the dead? Do the departed rise up to praise you? Selah

**12** Is your steadfast love declared in the grave, or your faithfulness in Abaddon?

**13** Are your wonders known in the darkness, or your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?

**14** But I, O LORD, cry to you; in the morning my prayer comes before you.

**15** O LORD, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?

**16** Afflicted and close to death from my youth up, I suffer your terrors; I am helpless.

**17** Your wrath has swept over me; your dreadful assaults destroy me.

**18** They surround me like a flood all day long; they close in on me together.

**19** You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness.

---
## Council Notes

SOPHIA detected **6** significant divergence(s) in Psalm 88.

- **88:2** — EMET preserves Hebrew word-order; LOGOS restructures for English clarity; PNEUMA interprets for contemporary application.

- **88:3** — EMET preserves Hebrew word-order; LOGOS restructures for English clarity; PNEUMA interprets for contemporary application.

## Translation Notes (Select)

### EMET
- **88:6**: 'Set-free among the dead' (bachofshy bammetim) — possibly 'released' to the realm of the dead; ironic 'freedom.'
- **88:11-13**: Five rhetorical questions — all expecting 'no' — pressing God: if the psalmist dies, there will be no praise from Sheol.
- **88:19**: Ends on 'darkness' (machshakh) — the only psalm that concludes without any note of hope or resolution.

### LOGOS
- **88:1**: Attributed to Heman the Ezrahite (cf. 1 Kings 4:31), making this one of only two psalms attributed to non-Davidic, non-Levitical authors (with Psalm 89/Ethan).
- **88:11-13**: The cascade of questions about death and divine forgetfulness is theologically bold: if God lets the psalmist die, God himself loses a worshipper. Self-interest and devotion merge.
- **88:18**: Psalm 88 is the darkest psalm in the Psalter — the only one that ends in unrelieved darkness. Its canonical inclusion validates lament without resolution as genuine prayer.

### PNEUMA
- **88:1-18**: This is the Bible's darkest prayer — bar none. It begins in darkness and ends in darkness. There is no resolution, no silver lining, no 'but God.' And yet it's included in Scripture, which means God accepts prayers that don't have happy endings.
- **88:19**: 'Darkness is my only friend.' That's the last word. The fact that this psalm exists in the Bible is itself a profound theological statement: you can bring your worst despair to God, even if nothing changes.

— SOPHIA
